To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DMSA scan findings in children with radiologically proven renal scarring after urinary tract infection were non-specific, and underestimated the individual scars.
DMSA scans are useful in the diagnosis of renal scarring, but the findings are non-specific and the scan may underestimate the number of individual scars.

the 99mTcc dimercaptosucinic acid (D.M.S.A) scan in patients who have had a previous urinary tract infection and in whom radiological scarring is present is of limited value in the assessment of renal scarring and should not be regarded as a definitive diagnostic investigation.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

DMSA scanning is of value in patients with radiologically diagnosed renal scarring but the results must be interpreted with great caution and should be correlated with the results of other imaging procedures.

DMSA scans are not necessary to confirm radiological evidence of renal scarring, but are of value in patients with established scarring to assess the extent and severity of renal damage, to detect additional scarring and to differentiate diffuse potentially transient from permanent scarring.
the DMSA renal scan is not an ideal method to diagnose and quantify scarring in the kidneys of patients who have had urinary tract infection in the past.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the DMSA renal scan is not the ideal investigation for detecting renal scarring.
DMSA scan should be performed in all patients with vesicoureteral reflux to detect renal scars, even if the patient has no urinary tract infection.
DMSA scans are not a substitute for intravenous urograms and should be used as a supplementary study in children with urinary tract infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DMSA scans are not always accurate and should be used as an adjunctive tool in the evaluation of the renal scarring.
the timing of any previous urinary tract infection must always be considered in order for a DMSA scan to be interpreted correctly.
DMSA scan findings in patients with established renal scarring may not always be specific and may underestimate the extent of the scarring.
